records.public_claim_text: Six proficiency levels are defined for literacy and numeracy (Levels 1 through 5 plus below Level 1) and five for problem solving in technology-rich environments (Levels 1 through 4 plus below Level 1).
records.public_claim_verbatim_quote: Six proficiency levels are defined for literacy and numeracy (Levels 1 through 5 plus below Level 1) and five for problem solving in technology-rich environments (Levels 1 through 4 plus below Level 1).

records.public_claim_text: Similarly to literacy, Finland and Japan report the highest numeracy scores, averaging at or above 290 points, and a majority of their adult populations score at or above Level 3.
records.public_claim_verbatim_quote: Similarly to literacy, Finland and Japan report the highest numeracy scores, averaging at or above 290 points, and a majority of their adult populations score at or above Level 3.

records.public_claim_text: The share of those scoring at or above Level 3 is 60% among tertiary-educated adults, but only 12% among those with below upper secondary attainment.
records.public_claim_verbatim_quote: The share of those scoring at or above Level 3 is 60% among tertiary-educated adults, but only 12% among those with below upper secondary attainment.

records.public_claim_text: In contrast, countries such as Chile, Switzerland and the United States have much lower literacy scores among adults with below upper secondary education and over 70% of low-educated adults at or below Level 1.
records.public_claim_verbatim_quote: In contrast, countries such as Chile, Switzerland and the United States have much lower literacy scores among adults with below upper secondary education and over 70% of low-educated adults at or below Level 1.

records.public_claim_text: This is true across different levels of educational attainment, with young adults (25-34 year-olds) scoring on average 15 points higher than older adults (45-54 year-olds).
records.public_claim_verbatim_quote: This is true across different levels of educational attainment, with young adults (25-34 year-olds) scoring on average 15 points higher than older adults (45-54 year-olds).

records.public_claim_text: In Germany and Switzerland, the gap is over 99 score points between young adults with tertiary education and those with below upper secondary education, showing pronounced inequalities in proficiency outcomes linked to educational background.
records.public_claim_verbatim_quote: In Germany and Switzerland, the gap is over 99 score points between young adults with tertiary education and those with below upper secondary education, showing pronounced inequalities in proficiency outcomes linked to educational background.

records.public_claim_text: Gender differences in literacy skills Gender differences in proficiency are generally small across OECD countries (OECD, 2024[1]).
records.public_claim_verbatim_quote: Gender differences in literacy skills Gender differences in proficiency are generally small across OECD countries (OECD, 2024[1]).

records.public_claim_text: The largest education-related proficiency gaps are observed in Germany, Switzerland and the United States, where differences exceed 106 points for men and 97 points for women.
records.public_claim_verbatim_quote: The largest education-related proficiency gaps are observed in Germany, Switzerland and the United States, where differences exceed 106 points for men and 97 points for women.

records.public_claim_text: The decline in literacy proficiency is most pronounced among those with below upper secondary education, where proficiency scores fell by an average of 17 points for younger adults and 20 points for older adults.
records.public_claim_verbatim_quote: The decline in literacy proficiency is most pronounced among those with below upper secondary education, where proficiency scores fell by an average of 17 points for younger adults and 20 points for older adults.

records.public_claim_text: These findings confirm the general pattern of skill attrition with age, which may reflect both natural cognitive decline and reduced opportunities for skill use (OECD, 2019[5]).
